title: One-take recording sessions
summary: The 1936 session of eight sides was cut in under three hours in one take each, as were the Troy Floyd records; a single mic and a wax disc forced one take, while other sessions allowed more.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Mm-hmm. Oh. We were listening to the record this morning again. Which one? The one with your own band from 36. What one? Which one? The whole. Oh, the whole album? All eight sides. Right, right. How did you feel at the end of the day?
After recording? Mm-hmm. Fortunately, this was cut in less than three hours.

How many takes did you have to do? One. Just a one-take shot? One takes, but that's all. And what about with the blues singers and with Troy Floyd? That was in 26 and 27. Yeah, how many takes did you have to do that? One.

It was almost a full session, but what happened, you would rehearse the number first and when you thought you had it, but then you were ready to go into the mic. One mic. And it was spelled on that record, this little black thing would come off and they'd pull it up and pull it up. Like a thread. Like a thread. One take.
You say forced issue, you mean that's all they encouraged you to take?
That's right. That's right. Forced issue. A little different.

Well sure it is. A lot different. For instance, when I recorded for Salt Man, I know one time we played, and we were going to take it. And by the same token, we made one cut on one of the sides with the hammer, I think it was. I can't recall the name of the song, but we hit that and offered one take. But the rest of them, two, three, like that.
